claims.text: The baseline is a powder-consolidated W–Cu composite without interfacial modification between the tungsten and copper phases.
Tungsten particles will be coated with a uniform 10–20 nm nickel layer before composite consolidation.
The nickel coating will create a graded interfacial region between tungsten and copper.
The nickel interlayer will bond the tungsten and copper phases more effectively than an unmodified interface.
Nickel provides an intermediate lattice structure between tungsten and copper.
Nickel provides an intermediate electronic structure between tungsten and copper.
The nickel interlayer will reduce thermal resistance at the W–Cu interface.
The nickel interlayer will facilitate electron transport across the W–Cu interface.
Reduced interfacial thermal resistance and improved electron transport will increase the effective thermal conductivity of the composite.
The nickel-coated W–Cu composite will have approximately 10–20% higher effective thermal conductivity than an otherwise comparable unmodified W–Cu composite.
The nickel-coated composite will retain mechanical strength similar to that of an otherwise comparable unmodified W–Cu composite.
The nickel-coated composite will retain irradiation resistance similar to that of an otherwise comparable unmodified W–Cu composite.
The predicted benefit applies under high-heat-flux, moderate-temperature, irradiation-stressed heat-dissipation and fusion-reactor joint conditions.
The benefit requires a uniform nickel coating optimized to approximately 10–20 nm thickness.
A nickel coating that is too thick or nonuniform could promote detrimental intermetallic-phase formation.
Such detrimental intermetallic phases could impair mechanical properties or irradiation stability.
The magnitude of the conductivity improvement and long-term irradiation stability may depend on coating-process parameters and post-processing heat treatments.
